lead: A coloured or ultraviolet-absorbing solution takes light out of a beam in proportion to how much substance it contains. Shine a known light intensity through it, measure what survives, and the Beer–Lambert law turns that measurement into concentration. Hospital laboratories use this daily for haemoglobin, bilirubin, glucose, creatinine and total protein. The instrument is a spectrophotometer; a colorimeter is its simpler cousin with a filter instead of a monochromator. This chapter explains the light measurement, the law, the instrument chain and the practical limits.
prereq: You need: concentration in mol/L, the base-10 logarithm, and the idea that a solution has a colour because it absorbs some wavelengths. The enzyme reactions that create colours for glucose are in Unit 4, Biosensors.

blocks.text: Visible light runs from about 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red); ultraviolet (UV) is the band below 400 nm. A solution looks coloured because it absorbs some visible wavelengths and lets others pass. A clear solution can still absorb UV. The laboratory uses both bands: visible for coloured reaction products, UV for proteins and nucleic acids.

Let I₀ be the light intensity entering the solution and I the intensity leaving it. Transmittance T is the fraction that survives. T has no unit and lies between 0 and 1; multiplying by 100 gives percentage transmittance, %T. Absorbance A is defined so that it grows as light is lost. The minus sign makes A positive when I is less than I₀. A is also called optical density (OD), though some older books use OD loosely.
T = I / I₀    and    A = −log₁₀ T = log₁₀(I₀ / I)
blocks.where: T is transmittance (no unit); I₀ is the incident light intensity; I is the transmitted light intensity; A is absorbance (no unit).

blocks.text: Absorbance is the useful quantity because it is linear in concentration. Transmittance is not. If a solution absorbs half the light, T = 0.50 and A = 0.30. If concentration doubles inside the linear range, T falls to 0.25 but A rises to 0.60, exactly double.

The law states that absorbance is proportional to concentration and to the light path. ε is molar absorptivity, a property of the substance at a stated wavelength and temperature. It is the absorbance of a 1 mol/L solution in a 1 cm cuvette. Because ε depends on wavelength, the instrument must be set to the same wavelength for standards and samples.

blocks.where: A is absorbance (no unit); ε is molar absorptivity in L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹; c is concentration in mol/L; l is the light path through the solution in cm.

blocks.text: A blank cuvette sets the reference. Fill it with the solvent or with reagent minus sample, set A = 0. This makes I₀ the light through the blank, so absorbance from the sample's colour alone is measured. Without a blank, the cuvette, solvent and reagent absorbances are wrongly added to the sample.

For routine work, prepare standards of known concentration, read their absorbances, and plot A against c. The line should pass through the origin with slope εl. Read the unknown from the line. The linear range is the concentration band where this line is straight. At high A (roughly above 1.5) stray light and molecular interactions bend the line; at very low A, noise dominates. Dilute and repeat if a sample reads outside the range.

A single-beam spectrophotometer has six parts in a row. The source gives polychromatic light. A tungsten-halogen lamp covers the visible band; a deuterium lamp covers UV. The monochromator, a prism or a diffraction grating, selects a narrow band of wavelengths. The cuvette holds the blank or sample. It is glass or plastic for visible light, but quartz for UV because ordinary glass absorbs UV. The photodetector converts transmitted light into current; a photodiode is common, and a photomultiplier tube (PMT) is used when light is very weak. The amplifier scales the signal, and the readout shows A and %T.

A colorimeter, also called a filter photometer, is the same chain with a coloured glass or interference filter in place of the monochromator. It works at a few fixed wavelengths, is cheaper and simpler, and suits a single routine test. A spectrophotometer can scan or select any wavelength in its range, so it is more flexible. Some syllabi call the whole topic photometry or colorimetry.

items: Switch on and let the lamp warm up.
Fill the blank cuvette and set A = 0 or %T = 100.
Wipe the sample cuvette and insert it.
Read A or %T. Handle cuvettes by the frosted sides, not the clear faces, and keep the light path free of bubbles and fingerprints.

blocks.text: In the clinical laboratory, spectrophotometry measures haemoglobin as cyanmethaemoglobin, bilirubin, glucose through an enzyme-produced colour, creatinine through the Jaffe reaction, and total protein by a colour reaction. Each test fixes a wavelength where the product absorbs strongly and the reagents absorb little.

Fluorescence spectroscopy, which some syllabi add, is a related method. The sample is excited at one wavelength and the emitted light is measured at a longer wavelength. It is more sensitive than absorption because the detector sees emitted light against a dark background, but it needs a fluorophore and careful correction for quenching.

An automated biochemical analyser uses the same Beer–Lambert law: it pipettes sample and reagent, incubates, reads absorbance in a flow-through or cuvette photometer, and computes concentration. See 3.5 Automated biochemical analysers. A flame photometer also measures light, but it measures emission from excited atoms, not absorption; see 3.2 Flame photometer.

figure.caption: The sample sits after the monochromator, so only the selected wavelength reaches it; the blank is read first to set 100 %T. The detector current is amplified and displayed as absorbance or transmittance.

spec.title: Single-beam spectrophotometer
spec.aria: Light from a lamp passes through a monochromator, then through the sample cuvette, and the transmitted light falls on a photodetector whose amplified signal is displayed as absorbance and transmittance.

examples.question: A 0.20 mmol/L standard of a coloured compound in a 1.00 cm cuvette reads A = 0.30. (a) Find ε. (b) A patient sample in the same cuvette reads A = 0.45; find its concentration. (c) What is the transmittance of the standard?
steps: Convert the standard concentration to mol/L: c = 0.20 mmol/L = 0.20 × 10⁻³ mol/L = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L.
Find ε from A = ε c l: ε = A / (c l) = 0.30 / (2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L × 1.00 cm) = 1500 L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹.
For the sample: c = A / (ε l) = 0.45 / (1500 L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹ × 1.00 cm) = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L.
Convert to mmol/L: 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L × 10³ mmol/mol = 0.30 mmol/L.
Find the standard transmittance: T = 10^(−A) = 10^(−0.30) = 0.50, that is 50 %.
examples.answer: ε = 1500 L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹; the sample concentration is 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L = 0.30 mmol/L; the standard transmittance is 0.50 (50 %).
examples.check:
A_std = 0.30
c_std_mmol = 0.20
c_std = c_std_mmol * 1e-3
l = 1.00
eps = A_std / (c_std * l)
print(eps)
A_sample = 0.45
c_sample = A_sample / (eps * l)
print(c_sample)
print(c_sample * 1e3)
T_std = 10 ** (-A_std)
print(round(T_std, 2))

traps: Forgetting the blank: reagent colour and cuvette absorption then add to the sample and give a falsely high absorbance.

Mixing up absorbance and transmittance: A is logarithmic, so doubling concentration doubles A but squares T: if A goes from 0.30 to 0.60, T falls from 0.50 to 0.25. The halving seen in one example is not a general rule. Both relations hold only inside the linear range.

Using a glass cuvette for UV work: glass absorbs UV strongly below about 340 nm, so very little light reaches the detector and the reading becomes noisy and distorted by stray light. If the sample cell is glass while the blank is quartz, the extra absorption is added to the sample and A reads falsely high. Use quartz, or UV-transparent plastic, for both blank and sample in UV work.
Assuming the calibration stays straight at high absorbance: above about A = 1.5, stray light bends the line; dilute the sample and repeat.
Changing the light path: A = ε c l, so a 0.5 cm cuvette halves A; standards and samples must use the same path length.

quiz.q: Define transmittance and absorbance, and give their symbols.
quiz.a: Transmittance T = I/I₀, the fraction of incident light that passes through the solution, with no unit. Absorbance A = −log₁₀ T = log₁₀(I₀/I), also with no unit.

quiz.q: Why is absorbance linear in concentration while transmittance is not?
quiz.a: Absorbance is defined as a logarithm, so the multiplicative loss of light becomes an additive quantity proportional to the number of absorbing molecules. Transmittance falls exponentially with concentration, so a plot of T against c is a curve.

quiz.q: A solution has transmittance T = 0.25. Find its absorbance.
A substance has ε = 2000 L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹. In a 1.00 cm cuvette its absorbance is 0.60. Find the concentration in mol/L.
A sample reads A = 2.0. Why is this value unreliable, and what should the technician do?
quiz.a: A = 2.0 is above the linear range; stray light and molecular interactions make the Beer–Lambert plot bend, so concentration read from a calibration line is wrong. Dilute the sample by a known factor, re-read, and multiply the result by that factor.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a blank cuvette, and what happens if it is omitted?
quiz.a: The blank contains solvent or reagent without sample. It sets I₀ and makes A = 0 for everything except the sample's colour. If omitted, absorbance from the cuvette, solvent and reagent adds to the sample reading and the concentration is overestimated.

quiz.q: State one difference between a colorimeter and a spectrophotometer.
quiz.a: A colorimeter uses a filter to select a few fixed wavelengths, while a spectrophotometer uses a prism or diffraction grating and can select or scan many wavelengths.

quiz.q: Inside the linear range, the concentration of a coloured solution is tripled. What happens to A and to T?
quiz.a: A becomes three times its old value: A_new = 3A_old, because A = εcl. Transmittance becomes the cube of its old value: T_new = 10^(−3A_old) = (10^(−A_old))³ = (T_old)³, that is T_old × T_old × T_old.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern laboratories use diode-array spectrophotometers that capture a whole spectrum in milliseconds, and microplate readers that read 96 or 384 samples at once. Point-of-care devices shrink the same optics onto a card for a single test. UV-Vis absorption is also the workhorse of water testing, pharmaceutical assay and food colour measurement. Search next for diode-array detectors, microplate readers and stray-light deviation from Beer–Lambert.
